title: System Architecture
description: How to structure systems: monoliths, microservices, layers, communication, scaling and caching.
resumo: Architecture = the decisions that are hard to change; start from the quality requirements, choose the simplest fit.
Monolith: one deploy, simple — keep it modular. Microservices: independent deploys, paid for with network, consistency and operations.
Microservices never share a database: each owns its data.
Layers: controller (HTTP), service (rules), repository (data); never skip the service.
Synchronous calls couple availability; messaging decouples and absorbs spikes. Beware the dual write — use an outbox.
Scaling out needs stateless services: sessions and files outside the instance (Redis, S3).
Cache with a TTL and eviction on write; local caches diverge across instances; never cache a balance.

subsections.subtitle: What Is Software Architecture?
subsections.formerSubtitle: O que é Arquitetura de Software?
subsections.description: The structural decisions that are hard to change later.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the first version is quick to build. A year later every change takes weeks, because everything depends on everything else.

**Concept:** software architecture is the set of important structural decisions: how the system is split into parts, how the parts communicate, where the data lives, and which qualities matter most — scalability, maintainability, availability, security, cost. These are the decisions that are expensive to change later, and each one is a trade-off.

**How it works:** start from the quality requirements (how many users, how often it changes, what can never go down) and choose the simplest structure that meets them. In a Spring Boot application, organizing packages by feature keeps each business area together and makes boundaries visible.
examples.code:
com.shop
 ├── orders      (OrderController, OrderService, OrderRepository, Order)
 ├── payments    (PaymentController, PaymentService, ...)
 └── catalog     (ProductController, ProductService, ...)

# Each feature package holds its own controller, service and repository;
# other features use only its public classes.
examples.interview_question: Why does software architecture matter in large projects?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Copying the architecture of a big tech company for a small team. Microservices, Kafka and Kubernetes for three developers and a few hundred users add operational cost without solving a problem you have.
examples.code:
WRONG: 3 developers, 500 users -> 12 microservices, Kafka, Kubernetes, service mesh
       most of the time goes into keeping the platform running

RIGHT: a well-structured monolith; split a part out when a real need appears
       (independent scaling, a separate team, a different release pace)

subsections.subtitle: Monolithic Architecture
subsections.description: One deployable unit with every feature.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a small team starting a product needs to ship quickly, test easily and deploy simply.

**Concept:** a monolith is a single deployable unit — one JAR, usually one database — containing every feature. It is simple to develop, test, debug and deploy, and calls between parts are plain method calls. The problems appear with size: long builds, everything deployed together, one module's bug or load affecting all of them, and many teams stepping on each other.

**How it works:** a modular monolith — clear internal boundaries, modules talking through public APIs — is often the best start, and can be split later where it is really needed.
examples.interview_question: Which scenarios favor a monolithic architecture?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: The "big ball of mud": any class uses any other class's internals, and modules read each other's tables. Nothing can change in isolation, and the monolith can never be split. Go through each module's public API.

subsections.subtitle: Microservices Architecture
subsections.description: Independent services, each owning its data.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** eight teams work on one monolith and wait for each other: one release train, one slow build, and on Black Friday the whole application must scale just for the checkout.

**Concept:** microservices split the system into small services, each owning one business capability and its own database, deployed independently and communicating over the network (REST or messaging). The benefits are independent deploys and scaling, and team autonomy. The costs are network failures, distributed data and consistency, observability across services, and much more to operate.

**How it works:** split by business capability (catalog, orders, payments), not by technical layer. Expect to need an API gateway, centralized logs and tracing, and a CI/CD pipeline per service.
examples.code:
┌─────────────┐
client ──▶ │ API Gateway │
           └──┬───┬───┬──┘
              ▼   ▼   ▼
       catalog  orders  payments    <- each one deploys independently
          │       │        │
         db      db       db        <- each one owns its data
examples.interview_question: What are the challenges of microservices compared with a monolith?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Microservices sharing a database. A column change in one service breaks the others, and they must deploy together — a distributed monolith, with all the costs and none of the benefits. Each service owns its tables; others use its API or events.
examples.code:
# WRONG
orders-service   -> shop_db.orders
payments-service -> shop_db.orders        # a column change breaks the other service

# RIGHT
payments-service -> GET orders-service/orders/42   (or consumes OrderPaid events)

subsections.subtitle: Layered Architecture
subsections.description: Controller, service and repository, each with one job.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** SQL in the controller, HTTP status codes in the repository: one change touches everything, and the rules cannot be tested without a database.

**Concept:** a layered architecture separates responsibilities: presentation (the controller turns HTTP into calls and results into responses), business (the service holds rules and transactions) and persistence (the repository reads and writes data). Each layer depends only on the one below it.

**How it works:** the controller is thin, the service does not know about HTTP, and the repository does not know about business rules. The service can then be unit-tested with a mocked repository.
examples.interview_question: How does a layered architecture make a system easier to maintain?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A controller that calls the repository directly. The business rules in the service are skipped for that endpoint, and the same rule ends up re-implemented (or forgotten) in the controller.

subsections.subtitle: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication
subsections.description: Direct HTTP calls or messaging between services.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** checkout calls the email service directly. When the email service is down, nobody can check out.

**Concept:** in synchronous communication (REST, gRPC) the caller waits for the answer: simple, but it couples availability — if the stock service is down, checkout is down too. In asynchronous communication, a service publishes an event to a broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ) and moves on; consumers process it at their own pace.

**How it works:** use asynchronous messaging for work that does not need an immediate answer — emails, invoices, stock updates — and to absorb load spikes. Use synchronous calls when the caller needs the answer now, always with a timeout.
examples.interview_question: When should you use messaging instead of HTTP calls between services?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Saving to the database and then publishing to the broker as two separate steps (a "dual write"). If the publish fails after the save, the event is lost and the other services never hear about the order. The Outbox pattern (Databases, advanced) solves it.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** traffic doubles. A bigger server works for a while, until there is no bigger server — and that one machine is a single point of failure.

**Concept:** vertical scaling means a bigger machine (more CPU and memory): simple, but with a ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling means more instances behind a load balancer: almost unlimited and tolerant to failures, but the services must be stateless — sessions, carts and uploads cannot live in one instance's memory or disk.

**How it works:** state goes to a database, a distributed cache (Redis) or object storage (S3), and authentication uses tokens instead of local sessions.
examples.code:
┌──────────────┐
clients ─────▶ │ Load balancer│
               └──────┬───────┘
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        ▼             ▼             ▼
    api (1)       api (2)       api (3)    <- identical, stateless instances
        └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                      ▼
            PostgreSQL + Redis (shared state)
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: State in the instance. With two or more instances, the next request may hit another one: the cart is empty, the uploaded file is not there.

subsections.subtitle: Caching
subsections.description: Lower latency and less load on the database.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the product page queries the database on every visit, even though the catalog changes a few times a day.

**Concept:** a cache keeps expensive results in memory — local (Caffeine) or distributed (Redis). The main risk is serving stale data, so set a TTL and evict the entry when the data changes (`@CacheEvict`). Cache data that is read often and changes rarely — catalog, configuration — never data that must always be exact, like a bank balance.

**How it works:** in Spring, enable caching once with `@EnableCaching`, then annotate methods. Without it, the annotations are silently ignored.
examples.interview_question: What are the risks of caching, and how do you invalidate a cache?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A local cache on several instances. A price update evicts the entry only on the instance that handled it; the others keep the old price until the TTL expires. Use a shared cache (Redis) for data that must be consistent, or keep the TTL short.
examples.code:
# 3 instances, each with its own Caffeine cache
updatePrice(42) -> handled by instance 1 -> evicted on instance 1 only
GET /products/42 -> instance 2 -> old price (until the TTL)

# RIGHT
spring.cache.type: redis       # one shared cache for every instance
